title: Color
instruction: Choose a surface first, then the text and graphic colors that pass on it.
intro: Oath & Action works in seven colors, and each one has a job. Newsprint, a warm off-white, is the page most of our work sits on, and Charcoal carries the words. Pillar Red marks the one thing a reader should see first in each view, meaning each screen, card, slide or printed page. The other four do narrower work: Prussian, our dark blue, holds panels of dates and figures, Stone draws hairlines, Verdigris, a muted green, shows success and focus, and White serves specimens and email.

Every pair in this chapter carries a contrast ratio, a measure of how far apart two colors sit in lightness, from 1 to 1 for a color against itself up to 21 to 1 for black on white. We measured each one on the exact colors our code names, by the formula in the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG).

rules.title: Cover most of every view in Newsprint.
rule: Every view keeps three limits. Newsprint covers 60 to 85 percent of it, each section holds one dark panel at most, in Charcoal or Prussian, and Pillar Red stays within 5 percent, signature red included.
The other shares in the palette sheet below, carried from our fifth edition, set the balance across a body of work, such as a month of stories or a whole report. A single view may fall outside them.

text: A warm, light page keeps long reading calm, and readers come to know Newsprint as ours before they read a word. A dark panel works as a signal only while it stays rare. Each one tells the reader the section has turned, for example from an explanation to the dates that follow from it.

correct.caption: One view at true size: a phone page about a school board vote. Measured from the rendered page, Newsprint covers 76 percent. Charcoal covers 18 percent as the one dark panel, the type and the rules, and Pillar Red 3 percent, counting the wordmark’s ampersand.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 05.1. The same page set on Charcoal and Prussian. Newsprint falls to 10 percent and dark surfaces take 86, so no panel can mark a turn. Every text pair here still passes 4.5 to 1, and the fault lies in how much of the view is dark.

specs.label: Dark panels in each section
specs.value: One at most, in Charcoal or Prussian

builders: Set a page’s ground with its surface class, such as .oa-surface-newsprint. The class points the short names, such as --oa-color-text-primary, at that surface’s tokens, so a panel changes surface with one class.

rules.title: Set text only on color pairs that pass.
rule: Text under 24 px, or under 18.66 px in bold, needs a contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 against its surface, and larger text needs 3 to 1. Take the primary and secondary text tokens for the surface. For any other pair, read its measured ratio in the tables below before you use it.

text: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) sets 4.5 to 1 for text and 3 to 1 for large text, which it defines as 18 point, or 14 point bold: 24 px and 18.66 px on screen. Readers with low vision need that margin, and so does anyone reading a phone in sunlight.

Stone, the secondary text color in our fifth edition, measures 4.29 to 1 on Newsprint. Secondary text on light surfaces now takes Deep Stone, Stone mixed 18 percent toward Charcoal, at 5.49 to 1. On dark surfaces it takes Dim Newsprint, Newsprint mixed 25 percent toward Charcoal, at 7.26 to 1 on Charcoal and 5.14 on Prussian.

correct.caption: The same short article on each surface at true size, body text at 17 px and captions at 14 px. Primary text measures 13.29 to 1 on Newsprint, 18.73 on White, 13.29 on Charcoal and 13.28 on Prussian; secondary text measures 5.49, 7.74, 7.26 and 5.14.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 05.2. The caption in Stone measures 4.29 to 1 and the red link 2.96 to 1, both under the 4.5 to 1 that 14 px text needs. A reader with low vision loses the caption first, and the red link spends the view’s one red on a line of small text.

builders: Choose the surface, then the role: secondary text on Prussian is --oa-color-text-secondary-on-prussian. Inside a surface class, --oa-color-text-secondary resolves to the same value. A pair with no token is a pair we have not measured, so add a token under Rule 05.6 before you use it.

rules.title: Give each view one working red.
rule: The wordmark’s ampersand and the lockmark’s lever are signature red and do not count, and neither do the ampersands inside the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge, which are identity marks. Each view (one screen, card, slide or printed page) then carries one working red, in this order of precedence: an error the reader must fix; the step a reader can take now; the one point the headline names, which in a systems figure is where a reform acts. One job may take several marks, such as each target of one reform. Red never sits on Prussian.

text: One red tells the eye where to go first. The order settles which mark gets it when two compete: a reader has to fix an error before taking a step, and a step a reader can take matters more than a point we want to make. Signature red is part of the marks themselves, so it never competes with the working red.

Red never sits on Prussian, where it measures 3.19 to 1 and reads as a party pair of red and blue. On Newsprint it measures 2.96 to 1, so a working red mark there takes a keyline, a 1 px Charcoal edge drawn inside the mark (Rule 05.5).

correct.caption: One view at true size, with two reds. The wordmark’s ampersand is signature red and does not count. The button is the working red: Sign up to speak is the step a reader can take now. The hinge divider’s ampersand takes Charcoal, the ink of Newsprint. The dates sit on a Charcoal panel, and 24 px of Newsprint part it from the red button.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 05.3. Three jobs share the red: the date in the headline, a bar under it and the button. The eye has nowhere to land first, and the red date also fails 3 to 1 as large text.

corrective.caption: When the reader’s entry has an error, the error takes the view’s red and the ask steps down to the Charcoal primary button until the reader fixes it. The red is the 4 px bar beside the field and the message, and the error mark draws in the text’s ink (Rule 11.15). The message sits on the Error Band, where Charcoal text measures 11.89 to 1.

specs.label: Working red, first claim
specs.value: An error the reader must fix, shown by the 4 px red bar beside it

specs.label: Working red, second claim
specs.value: The step a reader can take now

specs.label: Working red, third claim
specs.value: The one point the headline names

specs.label: Signature red on Newsprint, White and Charcoal
An icon that stands alone
specs.value: An icon’s red accent counts as signature red when the icon stands alone, as an app tile, an avatar or a single feature icon.

specs.label: Icons in a row or a menu
specs.value: In a row or a menu, icons go one color and only the current one keeps its red, and that red counts as signature red.

specs.label: The hinge diagram
specs.value: The hinge diagram never shares a view with the wordmark and never stands in for the hinge divider.

specs.label: A hinge headline
specs.value: A hinge headline’s ampersand uses the view’s working red.

specs.label: Hinge divider ampersand
specs.value: The hinge divider’s ampersand takes its surface’s ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian.

specs.label: Keyline on a red mark on Newsprint
Ask label
specs.value: White on Pillar Red, 4.17 to 1, 19 px bold or larger

specs.label: In this guide
specs.value: In the guide itself, specimens, labeled failure cases and palette swatches do not count.

builders: Count the reds before you ship a view. Mark each red element with data-red: signature for the marks, working with data-red-job for the one job. The shared check fails a view with two working jobs or any red over Prussian. When an error appears, swap the ask to --oa-component-button-primary-fill-on-newsprint.

rules.title: Show every state with a word or a shape as well as a color.
rule: Each interface state, from hover to error, changes its text or its shape along with its color. A disabled control stays readable and says what will make it available. State colors are their own set, kept apart from identity color and from the chart palettes in chapter 14.

text: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.1 Use of Color asks that a state show something besides color, and 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast asks 3 to 1 for the edges and focus rings that show one. Pillar Red and Verdigris measure 1.14 to 1 against each other, so a red error and a Verdigris success look alike to many readers unless a word and a glyph differ too.

correct.caption: Ten states on Newsprint at true size, each with its cue. The focus ring measures 3.37 to 1 and the warning mark 13.29. The error mark draws in the text’s ink, and the error’s red is its 4 px bar. Nothing here uses opacity. Rule 17.8 draws all ten on Newsprint and on Charcoal, and its plate is the reference for each.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 05.4. Two tracker rows that differ only by the hue of a dot. The dots measure 1.14 to 1 against each other, and in grayscale they print as #5F5F5F and #717171, two near grays that say nothing about which row has the problem. Rule 11.2 gives each tracker state a shape and a word.

specs.label: Focus ring on light surfaces
specs.value: Verdigris, 2 px, 2 px gap; 3.37 to 1 on Newsprint

specs.label: Focus ring on dark surfaces
specs.value: Newsprint; 13.29 to 1 on Charcoal, 9.42 on Prussian

specs.label: Selected
specs.value: A check before the word, the word in bold and a 2 px edge; in a list, the selected band, its 4 px bar and bold words (Rule 17.10)

specs.label: Disabled
specs.value: Deep Stone text and dashed edge, 5.49 to 1, with a reason line

builders: Change two things in every state: the color and either the words or the shape. Use aria-disabled="true" so a disabled control keeps its focus and its reason line can be read. Never fade a control with opacity; take the state token instead. Draw a state’s bar as a border, such as border-left: 4px solid. Forced colors, a setting such as the contrast themes in Windows that repaints a page in a few system colors, keeps a border and removes an inset shadow.

rules.title: Keep marks that carry meaning at 3 to 1.
rule: An icon, a chart mark, a control’s edge or a focus ring needs a ratio of 3 to 1 against its surface. Pillar Red measures 2.96 to 1 on Newsprint, so a red mark that carries meaning there takes a 1 px Charcoal keyline. The error bar takes none, since the error mark and the word “Error:” carry the error and the 4 px bar beside them repeats it. Stone passes for marks on light surfaces, and a hairline that carries no meaning may sit lower.

text: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast asks 3 to 1 for the parts of a graphic a reader needs and for the edges of controls. The keyline gives a red mark an edge the eye can find, at 13.29 to 1, and the fill keeps its red. Stone context bars measure 4.29 to 1, so they pass without help.

correct.caption: A finding at true size, 600 px wide. The bar the title names takes the view’s working red with a 1 px Charcoal keyline at 13.29 to 1; the other sectors stay in Stone at 4.29 to 1.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 05.5. Without its keyline the red bar measures 2.96 to 1 against Newsprint, under the 3 to 1 a mark needs, and its edge softens into the page.

specs.label: Keyline on red
specs.value: 1 px Charcoal border, inside the mark

specs.label: Error bar
specs.value: 4 px Pillar Red with no keyline; the error mark and “Error:” carry the error

builders: Draw the keyline as a 1 px border with box-sizing: border-box in HTML, as chapter 18’s ask does with --oa-component-button-ask-keyline-on-newsprint, or as a 1 px stroke on an inner path in SVG, so the mark keeps its size. Forced colors keeps a border and removes an inset shadow. On White and Charcoal, where red measures 4.17 and 4.49 to 1, a red mark needs no keyline.

rules.title: Give each tint one named job, and keep tints off identity marks.
rule: A tint is one palette color mixed toward Newsprint or Charcoal by a recorded amount, for one job. It enters only as a token, with its measured ratio. The wordmark, the ampersand, the lockmark and the pillar icons stay in solid palette colors, and no color on a page comes from lowering opacity.

text: Our fifth edition said “There are no tints.” Charts, error messages and selected rows need lighter and darker steps that no palette color supplies, so Edition 06 allows a tint that meets five conditions: a measured need, a recorded mix, one job, a passing ratio on every surface it serves and a registered token.

We mix in OKLab, a color space where equal steps look equal, which keeps a tint’s hue steady as it lightens. Opacity gives up that control. Charcoal at 40 percent on Newsprint measures 2.48 to 1, where the Deep Stone token measures 5.49.

correct.caption: Six of the token set’s tints, each with its recipe, its one job and its measured ratio. The set holds three derived colors and 29 chart tints; chapter 26 lists every one.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 05.6. The date line is Charcoal at 40 percent opacity, a gray no token names. It measures 2.48 to 1, under the 4.5 to 1 its text needs, and its color changes with whatever sits behind it.

specs.label: Deep Stone
specs.value: #4E535B, Stone 18% toward Charcoal; 5.49 to 1 on Newsprint, 7.74 on White

specs.label: Dim Newsprint
specs.value: #A3A19C, Newsprint 25% toward Charcoal; 7.26 to 1 on Charcoal, 5.14 on Prussian

specs.label: Error Band
specs.value: #E1C9C1, Pillar Red 88% toward Newsprint; Charcoal text 11.89 to 1

builders: Write a new tint as a recipe in the token source, such as mix('stone', 'newsprint', 0.70), and keep hex values out of pages. The generator computes the hex and every ratio, and the rule test fails a tint with no registered need. In CSS the same mix is color-mix(in oklab, var(--oa-color-palette-stone), var(--oa-color-palette-newsprint) 70%).

rules.title: Set charts and the atlas on Newsprint, in the chart palette.
rule: Newsprint is the page color for charts and the atlas. The series a title names takes Charcoal, and every other series takes Stone. When the title names one point, such as a single bar, that point takes the view’s working red with a Charcoal keyline, as in Rule 05.5. Values that rise and fall from a midpoint take the diverging scale, which runs from Prussian through a pale middle to Verdigris, with an arrow or a printed sign for the direction. Every party takes one neutral ink, with its name printed on the mark.

text: Neither end of the diverging scale belongs to a party, so a reader sees a rise or a fall before any side. A scale from red to blue reads as a party split in the United States, and Rule 01.3 keeps it out of our charts. Both ends of our scale print as dark grays, so the arrow carries the direction for any reader who cannot tell the hues apart. On Newsprint, a chart shared on its own still reads as ours.

Chapter 01’s one standard of evidence also decides which charts run. Charts are chosen by the question and the evidence. Every title is read from the left and the right to check that its words are accurate and fair. A set never adds or drops a finding to even the score.

correct.caption: The chart palette on Newsprint at true size: four roles, the diverging scale with its boxed arrows, the same scale in grayscale and the sequential Verdigris steps. Every label on a fill passes 4.5 to 1. Chapter 14 holds the full chart palette, with the dark ground and the grayscale proofs of each chart.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 05.7. A scale from red to blue, which Rules 01.1 and 01.3 keep out of our charts, reads as Republican against Democratic before anyone reads its key, and it spends the view’s red on every rising cell.

specs.label: The one point
specs.value: Pillar Red, 2.96 to 1, with a 1 px Charcoal keyline at 13.29 to 1

specs.label: Diverging scale
specs.value: Prussian, light Prussian, a pale midpoint, light Verdigris, strong Verdigris

specs.label: Labels on the diverging scale
specs.value: 13.28, 6.18, 11.76, 8.01 and 7.06 to 1, from Prussian to Verdigris

specs.label: Labels on sequential Verdigris
specs.value: 10.96, 7.81, 5.41, 5.20 and 8.27 to 1, from step 1 to step 5

specs.label: Neighboring steps under color-vision simulation
specs.value: At least 0.106 apart in OKLab, about 5 times the 0.02 that CSS Color 4 treats as the smallest visible difference

specs.label: Lightness in grayscale
specs.value: Ends at 0.31 and 0.46, the midpoint at 0.85, in OKLab lightness

specs.label: Party marks
specs.value: One neutral ink, the party’s name on the mark

specs.label: Measurements
specs.value: Our palette measurements on White, Newsprint and Charcoal, November 6, 2026

builders: Take chart colors from oa.chart.color, whose tokens follow the page color. The diverging scale exists on Newsprint only until a Charcoal ramp is measured. Print the value or the direction on every diverging cell.

extras.label: The seven colors
extras.caption: The seven colors with their values, jobs and shares across a body of work. The hex values are locked in our identity rules, and the shares come from our fifth edition.

extras.label: Color roles on each surface
extras.caption: Text-safe and graphic-safe roles on each surface. We measured every ratio against its surface on the token values. Text roles need 4.5 to 1, marks and edges 3 to 1, and hairlines carry no meaning.

extras.label: The ask on four surfaces
extras.caption: The ask on each surface at true size. White on Pillar Red measures 4.17 to 1, which passes only as large text, so the label never sets below 19 px bold. On Prussian the ask turns Newsprint.

extras.label: Every palette pair, measured
extras.caption: Every palette pair, measured. “Text at any size” means 4.5 to 1 or more; “Large text and marks” means 3 to 1 or more. Pillar Red never sets text, whatever its ratio.
